In the '90s we rode loose in the back of the station wagon, got left in the car while mom ran into the bank, and slept face-down in a crib full of blankets, and nobody thought twice. Half of it is flat-out illegal now. A cinematic recreation of the way it actually felt to be a '90s kid in a '90s parent's world. What did YOUR parents do that would get a phone call today? snippet.title: 13 Totally Illegal Things We Did to Get Music in the '90s
snippet.description:
Before Spotify, before iTunes, before you could just ask for a song — getting music in the '90s meant getting a little bit criminal. Taping off the radio. Burning CDs. That one friend with the fast internet and a LimeWire folder full of mislabeled MP3s. We all did it, and we didn't think twice.

This is a countdown of the 13 ways '90s kids "acquired" their music — the methods, the rituals, and the small daily crimes that defined growing up before streaming made it all legal and boring.

How many of these did you do? Be honest in the comments. 👇

snippet.title: What a 90s Arcade Actually Felt Like (Before They All Disappeared)
snippet.description:
You pushed open the door and it hit you all at once — the dark, the noise, a hundred machines screaming at the same time, and that glow.

The arcade was another planet. A cup of tokens that made you feel like a millionaire. The quarter balanced on the screen to call "next." The high-score initials of a kid you'd never met but somehow hated. The crowd gathering behind you when you got good.

Most of those rooms are gone now. This is what they felt like.

What was the machine you always went straight to? 👇

If you lived it, you already know. And if you didn't... you had to be there.

snippet.title: Gaming Before the Internet — One Console, One Couch, Three Friends
snippet.description:
Saturday. Raining. All four of you crammed onto one couch, in front of one TV, with one console between you.

This was gaming before the internet. No headsets, no usernames — the other players were right there, close enough to elbow. Winner stays on. Trash talk to your face. The pizza arriving. The friends you still remember decades later.
It was never really about the game. It was the excuse to be in the room together.

🔔 New trips back every week — subscribe and pull up a chair.
Who was on YOUR couch? Tag them. 👇

If you lived it, you already know. And if you didn't... you had to be there.

snippet.title: What It Felt Like to Rent a Video Game for the Weekend
snippet.description:
Friday afternoon. School's out. And there was only one place you wanted to go.

Before you owned a library of games, you rented them — one game, one weekend, and you'd better pick right. The wall of boxes. The empty case that meant it was already out. Playing it like the clock was running, because it was. And dropping it back in the box on Monday.

This is what it really felt like.

🔔 New trips back every week — subscribe and pull up a chair.
What's the one game you rented over and over? 👇

snippet.description:

snippet.title: Why You Never Felt Like You Fit In (The Generation Born Between Two Worlds)
snippet.description:
If you've spent your whole life feeling like you never quite fit — too young for one crowd, too old for the next, always half a step out of sync — this one's for you. And the reason isn't in your head.

If you were born somewhere between 1977 and 1985, you were the last kids raised in the analog world, and the first ones dropped into the digital one. You memorized phone numbers. You taped songs off the radio. You waited a week to find out if the photos came out. And then, as teenagers, you watched the whole world go online overnight.

You remember the before. You're the bridge between two worlds — and there's almost nobody left who can see both sides the way you can.
🔔 New trips back every week — subscribe and pull up a chair.

What's the one thing from the analog world you miss most? Drop it in the comments. 👇

If you lived it, you already know. And if you don't... well. You had to be there.

If you were born somewhere between 1977 and 1985, you were the last kids raised in the analog world, and the first ones dropped into the digital one. You memorized phone numbers. You taped songs off the radio. You waited a week to find out if the photos came out. And then, as teenagers, you watched the whole world go online overnight.

You remember the before. You're the bridge between two worlds — and there's almost nobody left who can see both sides the way you can.
🔔 New trips back every week — subscribe and pull up a chair.

What's the one thing from the analog world you miss most? Drop it in the comments. 👇

If you lived it, you already know. And if you don't... well. You had to be there.

snippet.title: 10 Things '70s Parents Did That Would Be Illegal Today
snippet.description:
Back in the '70s, a kid left the house at sunrise, rode loose in the back of a station wagon, drank straight from the garden hose, and didn't come home until the streetlights buzzed on — and nobody thought twice about it.
Do half of it today and you're getting a knock on the door.

In this one we walk back through the everyday stuff '70s parents did without blinking — the no-seatbelts, the way-back, gone-all-day, smoke-filled-car, lawn-dart, walk-to-school world — that would land you in a world of trouble now. Plus a few more I just couldn't leave out.

It's not that they didn't love us. They just figured a little danger built character. And somehow, we turned out mostly fine.

If you lived it, you already know. And if you didn't... well. You had to be there.

What do YOU remember that didn't make the list? Drop it in the comments. 👇
